newsitem.title: USA: Megan's killer withdrew under childhood abuse - brother.
newsitem.headline: Megan's killer withdrew under childhood abuse - brother.

text.p: Jesse Timmendequas, who raped and murdered 7-year-old Megan Kanka three years ago, became withdrawn under childhood abuse from his father, his brother testified Wednesday in the penalty phase of the trial.

Timmendequas was convicted last month of The 1994 attack on Megan, which terrified a community and inspired "Megan's Law." It required child molesters to register with police when they moved into a town and was much copied around the nation.

In a move defence lawyers hope will keep his brother from being executed, Timmendequas' younger brother Paul said in videotaped testimony that Jesse was "an open kid" before he began to be sexually and physically abused by their father.
"If you ran from the man you ended up with a lot of bruises on your body," Paul Timmendequas, 33, said in the one-hour videotape.
The tape was made several months ago. The Newark Star-Ledger newspaper quoted Paul Timmendequas Sunday as saying he would like to help execute his brother.
Once the abuse started when Jesse was 7, the boy "caved in on himself and stopped talking to anyone," his brother said.

Jesse Timmendequas, 36, avoided looking at courtroom television monitors as jurors watched intently. The videotape was prepared by Carol Krych, a defence witness and forensic social worker hired by Timmendequas' lawyers to investigate his background.

Timmendequas' lawyers hope they can keep him off death row by portraying his childhood as one filled with sexual and physical abuse that left him mentally ill. If not sentenced to die, he would spend the rest of his life in prison without parole.
The sentencing phase of the trial was expected to last several more days.
Timmendequas was convicted last month of raping, sodomizing and killing Megan. He was a twice-convicted sex offender who lived across the street from her.
The crime in New Jersey's Hamilton Township touched off a public outcry. Megan's parents said they had not known their neighbour's background.
Megan's Law originally required such offenders to register with authorities and empowered authorities to notify the public about those they regarded as posing the highest risk.
However, a series of rulings left the state with the power to require registration but not to notify the public, and that aspect of the law is being challenged in federal court.
Most other states also have versions of Megan's Law. In 1996 President Clinton signed a federal law making it easier for residents to get information about released sex offenders.
